headings.title: Introduction to Emergency Obstetric Care
headings.content: Emergency Obstetric Care (EmOC) encompasses a set of life-saving interventions designed to manage complications arising during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period. In the context of Nigeria and global healthcare, maternal mortality remains a critical public health challenge, largely driven by delays in recognizing complications, delays in reaching healthcare facilities, and delays in receiving adequate care at the facility level. As nursing students, understanding EmOC is vital because nurses are often the first line of defense in identifying high-risk conditions and initiating timely interventions. The framework of EmOC is structured to dramatically reduce preventable maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality by ensuring that women experiencing severe complications have access to timely, high-quality, and evidence-based clinical management. Effective EmOC integration into maternal and child health nursing empowers clinicians to recognize subtle clinical changes, such as early signs of postpartum hemorrhage or pre-eclampsia, before they escalate into life-threatening emergencies. By mastering these principles, student nurses prepare themselves to contribute significantly to the improvement of maternal health indices in Nigeria, fulfilling both national health goals and international sustainable development targets.

headings.title: Levels of Emergency Obstetric Care Facilities
headings.content: Emergency Obstetric Care facilities are broadly categorized into two levels: Basic Emergency Obstetric Care (BEmOC) and Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric Care (CEmOC) facilities. BEmOC facilities are typically primary health care centers or health posts where specific signal functions are performed to stabilize patients. These functions include the administration of parenteral antibiotics, uterotonic drugs, and anticonvulsants, manual removal of the placenta, removal of retained products of conception, assisted vaginal delivery (such as vacuum extraction), and neonatal resuscitation. On the other hand, CEmOC facilities are usually secondary or tertiary hospitals equipped to handle more complex, severe cases. In addition to performing all the BEmOC functions, CEmOC facilities possess the capacity to execute two critical advanced functions: performing life-saving surgeries, specifically cesarean sections, and providing safe blood transfusion services. For nursing students, it is essential to know these distinctions because patient outcomes depend heavily on appropriate referral pathways. Recognizing whether a primary health center can manage a bleeding patient or if an immediate transfer to a CEmOC facility is warranted can mean the difference between life and death for a parturient woman in resource-constrained environments across Nigeria.

headings.title: Major Direct Obstetric Complications
headings.content: Major direct obstetric complications are life-threatening medical events that occur directly during pregnancy, labor, or the puerperium, and they are the leading causes of maternal mortality worldwide. The primary direct complications include obstetric hemorrhage (both antepartum and postpartum), pregnancy-induced hypertension disorders such as pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, obstructed labor, sepsis, and complications from unsafe abortion. Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is particularly acute, frequently resulting in rapid hypovolemic shock and death if uterotonics and fluid resuscitation are delayed. Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia can lead to cerebral hemorrhage, multi-organ failure, and maternal convulsions, necessitating vigilant blood pressure monitoring and magnesium sulfate administration. Obstructed labor, common in settings with restricted access to timely operative delivery, can cause uterine rupture, severe maternal exhaustion, fistula formation, and fetal demise. Puerperal sepsis results from ascending infections following prolonged rupture of membranes or unsterile vaginal examinations. Nursing students must recognize the clinical presentations of these complications, such as unyielding vaginal bleeding, sudden visual disturbances, high fever, or prolonged cephalopelvic disproportion, to institute prompt life-saving nursing actions and collaborate effectively with the medical team.

headings.title: Signal Functions of Emergency Obstetric Care
headings.content: Signal functions of Emergency Obstetric Care are standardized, critical medical interventions used to identify and evaluate the quality, availability, and utilization of EmOC facilities. There are seven signal functions for Basic EmOC and nine signal functions for Comprehensive EmOC. The seven basic signal functions are: 1) administering parenteral antibiotics, 2) administering uterotonic drugs (such as oxytocin), 3) administering parenteral anticonvulsants for pre-eclampsia/eclampsia (such as magnesium sulfate), 4) performing manual removal of the placenta, 5) performing removal of retained products of conception (e.g., manual vacuum aspiration), 6) performing assisted vaginal delivery (vacuum extraction), and 7) performing neonatal resuscitation using a bag and mask. Comprehensive EmOC includes all seven basic functions plus two additional advanced functions: 8) performing surgery (cesarean section) and 9) providing blood transfusion services. For student nurses, memorizing and understanding these signal functions is crucial because they form the operational checklist for emergency readiness. When working in maternity units, nurses must ensure that all drugs, sterile instruments, and resuscitation equipment corresponding to these signal functions are fully stocked, checked daily, and ready for immediate deployment during an acute obstetric crisis.

headings.title: Initial Nursing Assessment and Triage
headings.content: Initial nursing assessment and triage in obstetric emergencies require speed, accuracy, and adherence to systematic protocols to identify life-threatening conditions within minutes of a patient's arrival. Using the ABCDE approach (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure) adapted for obstetrics, the triage nurse evaluates vital signs, level of consciousness, and active symptoms. Special attention is given to key red-flag indicators: severe vaginal bleeding, systolic blood pressure of 160 mmHg or higher or diastolic of 110 mmHg or higher, severe frontal headaches with visual disturbances, convulsions, high fever, severe abdominal pain, and absence of fetal movements. The nurse must quickly assess gestational age, parity, and the stage of labor if applicable. Immediate prioritization is essential; a woman presenting with signs of impending eclamptic seizure or profound postpartum hemorrhage bypasses routine registration and is escorted directly to the resuscitation bay. Effective communication using structured handover tools ensures that the entire multidisciplinary team is immediately aware of the patient's status. For nursing students, mastering rapid triage means developing clinical intuition backed by strict adherence to emergency algorithms, ensuring that no parturient patient is left unobserved during the critical golden hours of a crisis.

headings.title: Immediate Nursing Management in Obstetric Emergencies
headings.content: Immediate nursing management in obstetric emergencies focuses on stabilization, halting pathological processes, and preparing the patient for definitive treatment. For obstetric hemorrhage, immediate actions include calling for help, establishing large-bore intravenous access (16G or 18G), infusing warmed crystalloid fluids, drawing blood for hemoglobin, cross-matching, and coagulation studies, and administering prescribed uterotonics such as oxytocin, ergometrine, or misoprostol. Continuous monitoring of vital signs, fluid balance via an indwelling urinary catheter, and quantifying blood loss are mandatory nursing duties. In cases of pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, the nurse must ensure a patent airway, administer loading and maintenance doses of magnesium sulfate following strict safety protocols (checking patellar reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output), and provide a safe, padded environment to prevent injury during seizures. For shoulder dystocia or cord prolapse, the nurse assists with rapid postural maneuvers (such as McRoberts maneuver) and relieves pressure on the presenting part while expediting transfer to theater. Student nurses must practice these maneuvers and drug calculations rigorously, as quick, confident execution directly influences maternal and fetal survival.

headings.title: Inter-Professional Collaboration and Emergency Referral
headings.content: Inter-professional collaboration and safe emergency referral are essential components of comprehensive obstetric care, particularly when managing complex cases that exceed the scope of primary health facilities. Obstetric emergencies require seamless teamwork among nurses, midwives, general practitioners, obstetricians, anesthetists, and laboratory scientists. Clear, concise communication using standardized frameworks such as SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) ensures that vital clinical information is accurately conveyed during handovers and emergency consultations. When a patient requires transfer from a BEmOC facility to a CEmOC facility, the referring nurse plays a pivotal role in stabilization and preparation. Stabilization must occur prior to departure—meaning IV lines are secure, catheters are draining, bleeding is controlled or compressed, and convulsive crises are managed. Furthermore, the nurse must ensure that an appropriately trained healthcare provider accompanies the patient with emergency medications, oxygen, and resuscitation gear. Documenting the referral reason, vital signs, and treatments administered is legally and clinically mandatory. Student nurses must appreciate that effective teamwork bridges the gap between community clinics and tertiary centers, dismantling delays in specialized care.

headings.title: Post-Resuscitation Care and Complication Prevention
headings.content: Post-resuscitation care and complication prevention are critical final phases that safeguard the mother and newborn after surviving an acute obstetric emergency. Once the immediate crisis is resolved, the nursing focus shifts toward continuous monitoring, restoring physiological homeostasis, preventing secondary complications, and providing psychological support. Nurses must vigilantly monitor vital signs, uterine involution, lochia amount, urine output, and wound sites to detect early signs of secondary hemorrhage, surgical site infection, or acute kidney injury. Thromboembolism prophylaxis, early mobilization, and adequate nutritional support are initiated as appropriate. Complications like postpartum hemorrhage or severe pre-eclampsia can also trigger emotional trauma; therefore, compassionate, empathetic nursing communication and trauma-informed care are vital to address maternal anxiety, depression, or post-traumatic stress. Additionally, thorough documentation of the entire emergency event, interventions, and patient responses is legally required. For nursing students, mastering post-resuscitation care ensures that recovery is holistic, reducing long-term morbidity and supporting the mother's transition into successful motherhood and newborn bonding.
